subtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF CONCLUSION OF FIRST WORLD WAR
ANNIVERSARY OF CONCLUSION OF FIRST WORLD WAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before this house meets again the world will have marked the fiftieth anniversary of the conclusion of world war I, the war intended to end all wars. It is therefore appropriate, I suggest, that we pause a moment this morning to reflect on the sacrifices made by Canadians in that holocaust, and reflect as well on the minute distance which man has advanced in the past half century toward the goal of a warless world.

Monday next will be dedicated to the memory of the sacrifices and the assistance offered generously by Canadians during the war of 1914-1918 and other conflicts in which we have participated since then. Let us not forget, however, that this contribution also provides a lesson: that war is a poor solution and that it proves mainly the refusal of peoples to solve their conflicts with their intelligence. And let us not forget that war, in this atomic age, constitutes in the words of Albert Schweitzer "the height of absurdity".

When on Monday we pause in silent tribute to those who fell and those who served in the first world war I suggest, Mr. Speaker, we should remember that among them were members of the parliament of Canada. Their sacrifice will not be in vain if we here accept their challenge and strive to avoid the need for further sacrifices in the name of war.

subtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF CONCLUSION OF FIRST WORLD WAR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure all Canadians will join with the Prime Minister in the tribute he has paid today on the occasion of the fiftieth anniversary of the ending of the first world war. I think perhaps my deskmate the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) is the only veteran of that conflict who is still serving in this house.

subtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF CONCLUSION OF FIRST WORLD WAR

Hear, hear.
[DOT] (11:10 a.m.)

subtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF CONCLUSION OF FIRST WORLD WAR
speechtext:
I am sure all veterans will appreciate the recognition the Prime Minister has given today to their contribution, and to the contribution of those of their comrades who are not here to acknowledge that recognition on their own behalf.
While Remembrance day originally was set aside to honour the memory of those who fought and especially those who fell during the first world war, it equally commemorates those Canadians who made the supreme sacrifice for their country in the second world war and in the Korean conflict.
The Prime Minister in his statement has referred to the futility of war as a means to resolving disputes. Certainly in recent months we have been reminded that to resort to force is not a thing of the past but is still with us. In this imperfect world the choice men face is not always, or even very often, between good and evil but rather is a choice between two evils. The wars of this century in which Canadians and men of other countries gave their lives for freedom may be regarded by some as futile, but we owe even the imperfect order and peace we have today to their sacrifice. Their sacrifice at the very least gave mankind a further chance to seek the rational solution to which the Prime Minister referred.
In these days, when many Canadians are rightly concerned about the unity of our country, it is well to remind ourselves of those who gave their lives for its survival. I speak for Her Majesty's loyal opposition in seconding the remarks of the Prime Minister, and I am sure I can also presume to speak for the veterans of two world wars and of the Korean war in acknowledging the recognition paid to them this morning by the Prime Minister.

subtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF CONCLUSION OF FIRST WORLD WAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, obviously no one can say enough about the bravery and sacrifices of Canadian men and women in the first world war which ended 50 years ago, and their sacrifices in the war which ended 23 years ago. Our tribute to them is deep and humble.
I want to suggest that it is not enough merely to recognize that war is the ultimate in folly. If I may make a personal reference, I was five years old when the first world war broke out. I was living in a little village in eastern Europe. During that war it was sufficient for my family and others to avoid the consequences of the fighting by hiding in a cellar. That was no longer sufficient in the second world holocaust, and if another war should come there will be no place which will be safe for any human being.
I suggest that when we as parliamentarians pay heartfelt deep tribute for the sacrifice of the men and women in the wars of this century which enables us to continue to live in democratic freedom, we as parliamentarians should remember that war is not something that happens; war is the result of imperfect political action, and of the failure of political leaders. The first world war was the result of political and economic rivalry. The second was a result of the failure of the world to understand the dangers of nazism and the fact that Hitler received support from high places in many parts of the world.
I urge, Mr. Speaker, that as we pay tribute to our dead in the world wars of this century we look carefully at the political international situation today, in which we have pursued policies which may well lead not merely to another war but to the total destruction of humanity.

subtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF CONCLUSION OF FIRST WORLD WAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the right hon. Prime Minister for having sent me, this morning, a copy of the statement he has just made. However, I regret one thing: that I received an English copy while I should have preferred a copy of the French version.
In any event, I echo the words of the right hon. Prime Minister to the effect that wars have never solved anything and constitute "The height of absurdity". If only peoples and their leaders could convince themselves of this. Let us pay tribute to all those Canadians who sacrificed themselves for their country and let us hope that wars will forever be banished by all the peoples of the world. The

atomic age can destroy the universe or enable it to grow and prosper. Everyone wants peace, and it is our duty, as responsible parliamentarians, to achieve a just and lasting peace, within our country as well as abroad.

subtopic: NIGERIA-PROVISION OF CARIBOU AIRCRAFT FOR RELIEF FLIGHTS
NIGERIA-PROVISION OF CARIBOU AIRCRAFT FOR RELIEF FLIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I stated in the house on Monday of this week that one of the subjects which Professor Head had discussed with General Gowon was the most effective form of assistance which Canada might offer Nigeria respecting the distribution of relief supplies in federal territory. I said these discussions were being pursued on an official level and that I hoped to make a further statement shortly.
November 8, 19G8

I wish to say today that we have now concluded an agreement to make two Canadian Caribou aircraft available through the Canadian Red Cross to the Nigerian Red Cross for the distribution of relief supplies in federal territory. Because of the short range of the Caribou and navigational problems encountered in ferrying them the great distance involved, this operation is a complicated one, and I am informed they cannot be on the ground in Lagos for some 14 days.
It is the intention of the government to recall the Hercules aircraft now at Lagos which has been unable to operate because of the poor condition of the forward airstrips, a condition which will not hinder the operation of the lighter Caribou aircraft.

The result is that the first conferences held by this new government and its ministers under the leadership of the new Prime Minister have perhaps done more in the past few days and weeks to destroy any growth and understanding of federalism and national unity than what has occurred over a period of years.
I am interested in this particular phase of the development and appearance of the federal government at these conferences because of the different approach, views and ideology of the present Prime Minister from those he held when he was not a member of this house and did not hold the high office of Prime Minister. I refer to the years 1958-61 when the present Prime Minister, myself, David Lewis, Professor Frank Scott, Professor Michael Oliver of McGill University, Professor Grube of Toronto, Professor Jamieson of the University of British Columbia and Dr. Eugene Forsey, research director of the Canadian Labour Congress, were members of an editorial board charged with the drafting of a book "The Socialist Analysis of the Future of Canada". The book was published in 1961 and was called "Social Purpose For Canada". In this book-and this is marvellously coincidental with the approach of this government at the recent conferences in Ottawa-there is a chapter headed "Practice and Theory of Federalism". The author is Pierre-Elliott Trudeau.
I think the house would be most interested in the views and the ideology of the federalism that is Canada in the written word and in the government's attitude and actions in doing everything possible to break real federalism by means of the presentation of a fait accompli to the provincial premiers and their other ministers just a few days ago. I believe Hansard should have on record what the present Prime Minister wrote when he was jointly responsible with these other socialists for preparing a work on what is required for national unity and federalism in Canada. Just in case some hon. members might think I would take quotations out of context I will give the page numbers so that

they will be able to find them. They are indeed interesting, Mr. Speaker. As found on page 381, Pierre-Elliott Trudeau said:
From the foregoing analysis of the B.N.A. Act it is obvious that intergovernmental co-operation is not only possible but that it is in many ways constitutionally indispensable.
At page 385 we find these words:
And since the future of Canadian federalism lies clearly in the direction of co-operation, the wise socialist will turn his thoughts in that direction, keeping in mind the importance of establishing buffer zones of joint sovereignty and co-operative zones of joint administration between the two levels of government.
Again, at page 389:
Consequently the economic aspects of socialist theory might be a guide towards a more efficient distribution of powers under the constitution.
At page 389 we find the following: Consequently, in such matters-
Oh, this is a honey when we recall the meetings of these past few days and the government's presentation of hard of heart fait accompli-"This is it; take it or lump it."
-there is no reason to presume that the federal government will be more enlightened than the sum of the provincial governments, or even than one provincial government acting alone.
This most important view of Pierre-Elliott Trudeau was completely negated when ministers of the government of which he is Prime Minister met with the provinces a few days ago. I should like to refer to one more quotation which appears at page 392:
The basis of a socialist critique is to state clearly what the provincial governments can do and fail to do, and what the federal government can do and does not do, each within its respective jurisdiction.

We have had provincial conferences in the past and undoubtedly we will have more in the future. These representatives should meet as often as required in order to resolve these problems in the only conceivable way.
This can only be accomplished by a revision of the constitution whereby there is a clear line of demarcation between federai, provincial and municipal authority. As brilliant as the Fathers of Confederation were 101 years ago they could not foresee the problems of government and the demands of the people 101 years later. Nor could they possibly foresee that Canada would not have two levels of government but three-federal, provincial and municipal.
Temporary solutions may be found as a result of conferences. I should like to say it is my strong feeling that if we are realistic and sensible in our desire to resolve these problems we will exercise all the pressure we can on the government to adhere to the principle of bringing all levels of government together for as long as necessary to reach an understanding and a degree of co-operation in relation to the division of responsibility of the three levels of government, as well as fiscal jurisdiction. It is only when that has been accomplished that we will be in the position of knowing who is responsible in legislation and for taxation. Once this has been accomplished people will know which government is responsible for supplying necessary things. They will know the taxing powers of each level of government and which government must impose an extra tax to provide for certain demands. I feel this is a most important matter which has not been given proper consideration.
It is also my belief that if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) is correct and there will be an over-all policy and change in federal fiscal arrangements and a balanced budget, which many of us doubt, then consideration should be given to at least making a step in that direction. What has been our fiscal policy? In the main it has been to borrow for 20, 25 or 40 years and then pass on the refunding responsibilities to an unborn generation. On an ethical basis, as far as it is possible, when we borrow under our authority we should not only make provisions for paying the interest but should accept a responsibility for setting aside annually an amount of money so that at the end of the borrowing period we can pay off that debt.

It is a group of businessmen who organize themselves in order to make profits out of capital. There is a world of difference between the two terms of this comparison.

Unlike certain other organisations, a co-operative association should not have a tendency to become a capitalist concern. The aim of a co-operative association is simply to provide services.
That is why the ministers who work with the Minister of Finance and hon. members from Quebec should act immediately, as they did, for example, in order to restore the distribution of mail on Saturdays in rural areas, for the very survival of the institutions which
The Budget-Mr. Dumont we built with so many sacrifices is involved. Quebec and Quebecers will never, at a time when they are gaining strength, accept the disappearance of those organizations which are about the only property they have left.
Aside from the Desjardins movement, the Societe des Artisans-a life insurance company-and some other organisations such as the Laurentienne or the Catholic Farmers Union, what else really belongs to us, from the economic point of view? Why should we fight to defend this idea of the Minister of Finance whose aim is simply to destroy co-operative institutions?
The enemies of co-operatives often complain that the rate of taxation the government of Canada is imposing on company profits sometimes reaches up to 52 per cent. This is one way of deceiving the public at large. They keep repeating that companies are burdened by taxes and, that, in this respect, co-operatives are a greatly favoured economic sector.
I have on hand a document supported by figures which established that it is just the contrary which is the case. As it would take too much time to quote at length this 10-page document, I shall request the house to let me table this document to be included in Hansard so as to allow the Canadian people to know the amount of taxes private companies have paid comparatively to the amount paid by co-operatives. With the permission of the house, this document could be added in the appendix.

Corporate dividends, when added to personal incomes (salaries, wages, etc.), are not taxable at the rate of 23 per cent of their value. From the amount of 22 per cent of dividends, one can deduct 20 per cent of the net value of dividends received (see Exhibit "B").
For example, our shareholder should pay, apparently, $3,827 of the $17,394 received as dividends. But he may claim 20 per cent of that amount, that is $3,479; therefore, he has to pay only $348.
Therefore, the Crown levies $5,196 in income tax from an average company and $348 from the average shareholder, that is $5,544 altogether. If this amount is applied to the average net profits ($23,089) of the 10,819 companies, it can be seen that the Crown receives 24 per cent of those profits.
Companies and Co-operatives
Please note one thing before going further. If the company keep its profits, instead of paying dividends to its shareholders, taxes paid to the Crown decrease by $348 (amount of personal income tax) to approximately 22.5 per cent of the average net profits.
On the other hand, the same profits can be paid out by a co-operative to farmers, as a rebate. Therefore, the farmer with a taxable income of $4,000 (exclusive of rebates) pays income tax at the rate of 22 per cent of the rebate based on his purchases at the co-operative; it does not matter whether the rebate is cashed or left with the co-operative.
Capital gains
When an economic business does not pay dividends to shareholders, a time comes when its shares increase in value. When a shareholder sells his shares at a higher price than he paid for them, the difference between both prices is called a capital gain, which is tax-free.
To have an idea of the advantages to investors (and to economic companies, but not to co-operatives or to their members), let us take the example of an elevator factory.
In 1957, the shares of that company were selling for $23; now, quite recently, they had reached $96. One who bought some eleven years ago is now making a profit by selling them at $73 per share which is entirely tax-free.

The second table in the report of the Retailers' Association indicates that Ontario then had some 77,773 taxpayers and owners of
The Budget-Mr. Dumont retailing businesses not legally constituted. Together, they received an income (profits) of $420 million and paid $45.4 million in taxes (see exhibit "C").
In other words, the income of the average owner of such businesses was taxed at the real rate of 11 per cent, that is less than the rate applied to the rebates for purchases of farming implements granted to the farmer whose taxable income varies between $4,000 and $5,999.
Any accurate comparison is difficult
The statistical data quoted do not include the 5,420 retailing companies nor the 30,563 individual owners who did not pay any income tax in 1960, because the business was showing a deficit or its income was lower than the taxable level.
The statistical data and the examples quoted in this article are quite general, let us admit it, not because our information is inaccurate, but because we must stick to averages. In addition, a great number of variable factors come into account as to the incidence of the various regulations on corporate and personal income tax.

We have not taken in consideration up to now, it is true, the fact that an increasing proportion of the volume of consumers cooperatives take the form of personal and household assets and their rebates are not taxable.
This is the time to repeat it: it is not the purpose of the co-operative to increase the income of its members, but to reduce their expenses. It succeeds in doing so by refunding the difference between the cost price and the real cost of services provided.

The statistical data are based on 10,819 retail companies having paid taxes in 1960. On the whole, the profits of those companies reached $249.8 million, and their net taxable income (after deduction of the previous year's losses), $244.4 million. They paid altogether $86.8 million income tax (see Exhibit "A").
By dividing the total net profits ($249.8 million) by the number of companies (10,819), we see that each one has realized an average profit of $23,089 and that its net taxable income was $22,590.

As I said, if the budget carries as it is, it is obvious that the most heavily taxed will be the insurance companies as compared with trust companies, mutual fund companies and banks. Why should the minister not tax these institutions? He could get from them all the money he needs to satisfy his ever growing need for new funds.
At the same time, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) wants to levy income tax on these companies. This represents an amount almost equivalent to the tax levied on investment income. Still not satisfied, the Minister of Finance, when the policy holder redeems his policy or receives a gift or transfers his policy to another person, taxes the gain on the insurance policy. Here is how this works out: Redeemable value of the policy minus the net premiums paid or, in other words, the premiums paid after deduction of the accrued dividends. If this tax is not one on capital gains, I wonder what is. In a mutual fund company, for instance, there is admittedly an annual dividend and it is normally calculated on a rather low interest of 3 or 4 per cent. The true profit is obtained from the sale of the mutual fund policies. For example, if I were the owner of a mutual fund policy of $500 and, after a number of years, I sold it for $1,000, I would not be required to pay any tax on the capital gain accrued on this fund. In fact, this profit results solely or almost from interest which I should have been receiving during those years.
In my estimation, the whole thing is ridiculous, Mr. Speaker. A life insurance company is not a capitalistic institution whose aim is profits. On the contrary, these companies, especially the one belonging to Quebec or Canada are the property of the policy holders. I am speaking about most of the existing mutual and fraternal societies. Therefore, those companies belong in part at least to their policy holders. It is well known that most of the insurance policies are of the participating type. Also, the law provides that for companies of this type, the insured have a right to elect as beneficiaries a certain number of administrators in order to protect their interests. Therefore, even if the Minister of Finance includes the life insurance companies for taxation purposes, he is not in fact levying taxes from those companies but rather from the public generally, since undoubtedly the effect of this taxation reduces refunds or

DEBATES	November 8, 1968
dividends on existing insurance policies which in turn will result in higher premiums for new policies. Who is paying? It is surely the public generally. It is not a matter of taxing the corporations, but it involves the public generally and, certainly, the little people are the losers.
I wish to emphasize that I do not want the insurance companies to be state-owned. I want them to remain on a co-operative basis as they are at the present time, for we have in the province of Quebec the best example of what socialism will do. The nationalization of the hydro companies has simply resulted in increasing the electricity rates. This is a case where co-operative hydros would have been of great help, whereas nationalization has not produced any results. In other words, it is only through co-operation that results would have been obtained.
This morning I had begun to give an example of the difference between co-operatives and private enterprise in order to demonstrate the abuses by capitalism wherever there is a concentration of profits.
Encyclicals have been written in this respect. Only a co-operative is able to check those organizations which, too often, are bent on making profits but, as we always say, have no heart unlike co-operatives which can make people benefit from the profits they make. I said earlier today that for 18 years I have helped to set up co-operative organizations of this kind, because I found that money had a soul in those organizations. In a capitalist company where exploitation of people is carried to its maximum, we do not meet people who are thinking in terms of human beings, they are only thinking in terms of the profits they are making. This is the reason why, when there is concentration of wealth on a large scale, in addition to small enterprises which are successful-and we recognize their usefulness-we must set up co-operatives such as the ones we have established in Quebec over the last 25 years.
Let us go on with the comparison: in the co-operative organisations, savings remain within the consumer's community and his money keeps going around so that in the long run, everybody benefits by it. It happens only too often in some private companies who exploit people that their profits end up in the hands of businessmen abroad, as for instance in the case of Snow-Jet Company, at Thetford Mines, a company which is making a motor-ski specially designed, prepared, oriented and
November 8, 19G8	COMMONS
organized to be sold in the province of Quebec. This company, however, is now owned by Americans. Thus, wealth is concentrated in the hands of some capitalists who, later on, come and drain the economic blood of our people leaving us with little choice but to be water carriers or lumberjacks.
1 want to carry further my comparison: The co-operative is owned by the members under a democratic process, since every member has an equal say on the elaboration of policies. The co-operative belongs to the people. "One man, one vote." Everybody remember that truth. In private companies, the control belongs to the shareholder or shareholders who have the largest number of shares. The ownership of 51 per cent of shares represents a controlling interest, but money is the deciding factor in private companies. This is why co-operatives require that money be used in a more human way.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the course of the budget debate my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) said I would be intervening, and I do so now. I rise to speak today because of my particular interest in the performance of the Canadian economy from the point of view of the consumer whom it is my statutory obligation to represent.
The consumer interest lies in an economic system which makes available an increasing abundance and variety of goods that are dependable in quality and reasonable in price. Similarly, consumers who rely on the use of credit-and their numbers are ever-increasing-are concerned about interest rates and borrowing terms.
During the past three years we have seen an almost uninterrupted increase in Canadian prices. And in the past two years, as the
DEBATES	2593
The Budget-Mr. Basford Economic Council of Canada said in its fifth annual review:
Prices have been marching forward against consumers across a broader front than at any time in the past 15 years.
This has occurred despite the fact that over-all demands on our economy have eased somewhat since the middle of 1966 and despite the fact that unemployment has been running at higher levels than in 1965 and 1966.
In the last couple of years the consumer price index has been going up at approximately 4 per cent per annum. These price pressures have been accompanied by corresponding upward pressures in costs, including wage costs, salaries, interest rates and rents. I know there is a good deal of argument as to which is the cause and which is the effect. The businessman is inclined to put most of the blame on wage increases. The trade unionist tends to blame business for raising prices and thus reducing the real value of existing wages. I believe these are sterile arguments. The process is essentially a circular one; rising prices give rise to increasing cost pressures and higher costs in turn give rise to still higher prices. Moreover, there are many other sources of income and cost pressures in our economy-rents, professional services, interest, stock options, to cite a few examples.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
In any event, the effects are no mystery to the victims of inflationary forces. These victims are the Canadians who are old, who are poor, who have no means of adapting their circumstances to the rapid change. They are not organized to insist that their incomes reflect rising price levels. They have no power to insist on a fair share. Citizens who enjoy no bargaining power cannot bargain for a better deal. A fixed income should not mean a fixed injustice. There is always a danger that those whose market power is strong will be somewhat complacent about inflation. They are in a position to protect themselves, and those with little or no bargaining power are left to take the strain. The major instruments that governments must rely upon to keep the economic system in reasonable balance and to maintain reasonable price stability are fiscal and monetary policy. In the budget speech last week the Minister of Finance explained how this budget is intended to contribute to these purposes, and I shall not attempt to add to what he has said on this aspect of the matter.
November 8. 1968

The Budget-Mr. Basford
Without getting involved in conflicting schools of economic thought or theory, Mr. Speaker, it is generally accepted among economists that the basic influence on price performance and employment levels is aggregate demand in the economy. This is reflected in expenditure by consumers, by businesses, by governments, and by foreigners who buy our exports. The key to our performance lies in demand management as expressed in fiscal and monetary policies.
These have to be based on the best available judgment as to what businesses are likely to spend on their investment programs, what governments are likely to spend, and what our exports are likely to be. If the economic system were free from friction, rigidities, and time lags, and if we could foretell the future with more safety, the determination of the correct economic policies would be greatly simplified. The rudder, if we could set the rudder, would be set in the right position and, subject to occasional corrections for changes in the wind, the ship would remain steady on her course.
But we do not live, Mr. Speaker, in such a perfect world. Because of lags in the movement of impulses through the economy, responses to changes in the general economic environment take some time to develop. And what is more, changing expectations about future economic developments can have a perverse affect on the decisions of today. To put the matter more concretely, I think we are faced today with a situation in which a long period of expansion, the longest in our history, has created unusual expectations about future price increases and about continuing economic growth. These expectations are leading our businessmen and our trade unions to regard as normal rates of increase in prices, wages and other costs that are not consistent with reasonable price stability and are probably not sustainable. There is no doubt that these trends could be substantially slowed down, if not eliminated, by a very restrictive fiscal policy, but no one can say what level of unemployment and loss of potential output would be the result. We must consider other approaches.
Many industrial countries have been attempting in recent years to find ways of supplementing the major traditional instruments, fiscal and monetary policy. They have sought other measures to influence the movement of prices and incomes. Most hon. members will be aware of the efforts the British government has been making over a


number of years in this regard with the aid of a prices and incomes board, and the adoption of a set of fairly rigid guidelines.
The United States government has also tried programs in this field, first by setting voluntary guideposts, as they called them, for price and income behavior and more recently by creating a cabinet committee on price stability. This committee is charged with the task of looking into special situations such as supply bottlenecks in the economy and the like. A number of European countries have also experimented with various and different approaches to the same problem.
I wish I could tell the house, Mr. Speaker, that all these approaches have been successful, but the fact is that the results seem to have varied from country to country and from time to time. I do not think anyone would claim that these programs can do more than supplement and assist, in a modest way, fiscal and monetary policies. These policies remain the major influence on price and cost performance but there is a strong body of opinion that if the supplementary programs are judged by modest and realistic standards they have had some success.
As hon. members are well aware, the government has, over a number of months, been considering the introduction of a supplementary price stability program in Canada. This subject was studied by the Economic Council of Canada in 1965-66 at the request of the government. The council noted that a formal incomes policy was usually understood to comprise a set of general guidelines for incomes and prices in the whole economy, a means of making these guidelines relevant for individual price and wage decisions, and a means of inducing conformity with the guidelines. The Economic Council of Canada, concluded that a formal incomes policy would not be an effective way of bringing about an improved reconciliation of high employment and reasonable price stability in Canada under normal peacetime conditions.
I agree with the council's view that a formal incomes policy, so defined, would not be suitable in Canadian conditions. The question we have been studying is whether a less formal price stability program could make a contribution, a program which would involve the creation of machinery to provide better information about current trends in prices, costs and productivity, and to encourage greater restraint on the part of those responsible for price and income decisions. Such a
November 8, 1968	COMMONS
program could clarify for all of us the forces underlying our unsatisfactory price and cost performance, and could analyse special problem areas in our economy to see where improvements could be achieved. We have concluded that a program of this kind should be initiated.
A central element in this approach will be the creation of an independent public agency to study, investigate and report on problems of rising costs and prices. Its functions would include research and the issuing of periodic public reports on current developments in this field. There will need to be arrangements for parliamentary review of the reports of this agency. This role could be assumed by a parliamentary committee, perhaps the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs. We believe, Mr. Speaker, that this machinery, working together, could make a valuable contribution to greater understanding of the forces affecting our prices and costs, and bring home to all of us the need for social responsibility in price, cost and income decisions.
We have had some initial informal consultations about some of these ideas with provincial governments and with some business and trade union leaders. The government is now working on a white paper or policy statement which will contain some proposals and which will suggest possible means of implementation of this machinery. The white paper, which is being worked on now, will be available later this year. We shall be undertaking further, more formal consultations with interested parties. A program of this kind, however, will be only fully successful with broad support from business and labour or trade union groups. This support is crucial. This is why full consultation is essential before final decisions are taken as to the exact scope and nature of the program. The government will also wish to see the report of the task force on labour relations, or the Woods task force, before making final decisions, since this is one of the subjects the task force has had under consideration.
I know that some people, both in labour and in management, are less than enthusiastic about a program of this kind in Canada. Some, I believe, are inclined to judge it in advance on the assumption that it is the British program or the American program, or some other imported program. We have, however, to design a program that suits Canada's business and labour structure, that
DEBATES	2595
The Budget-Mr. Basford suits Canada's economy, open as it is to international forces, and that suits Canada's federal and parliamentary system of government. I hope people will refrain from pinning labels on this program, labels from other countries. There is no doubt at all in my mind that the public generally are strongly in favour of action by the government in this field of stabilization. I would urge members of interested groups to remain open-minded while we prepare our white paper and prepare for our consultations with them.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
The success of this program will depend heavily on the quality of those who serve on this new agency. We will be appealing, in the course of working out the policy, to able and experienced people from the universities and elsewhere, to come and give of their time by way of public service in support of a worthwhile cause.
I want to make it perfectly clear that this program will not involve any attempt to introduce price controls or controls on incomes. One merit of our mixed market economy is the way allocation of resources among all kinds of competing requirements is determined by a flexible price and income system. When consumers choose to buy more and more of a particular product their intervention in the market sets in motion price effects which draw more resources into the production and distribution of that product. Similarly a successful, efficient business is able to outbid less efficient businesses for skilled labour and other resources. Price and wage flexibility within the market economy must be maintained if we want, as we do, a dynamic and efficient economic system capable of producing steadily rising standards of living for Canadians, and capable of maintaining and expanding our position in world markets.
This is not to deny that there are special cases where some form of price regulation is desirable. Certain services and utilities, such as railroads and telephone companies, by their nature are more efficient as monopolies, at least for part of their operations. In these cases there is no alternative to the application of statutory rate controls, and where these services are within its jurisdiction parliament has acted to provide for the regulation of rates.
The remarks I have made about the role of the price system are based on the assumption that the system is reasonably competitive. To
November 8. 1968

The Budget-Mr. Basford the extent that there is monopolistic market behaviour, including collusion and other restrictive trade practices, the role of the market in allocating resources to their best uses is impaired. Moreover, prices that purchasers have to pay may be unreasonably high. The government must be concerned not only with maintaining a reasonable degree of price stability, but also with maintaining competitive market conditions, so that prices to consumers and other buyers will not be higher than they need be. This is the role of the Combines Investigation Act and of the small but dedicated group of officials who administer the act.
I have heard a number of allegations in this house to the effect that the combines act is not being enforced vigorously enough or broadly enough. The fact is that, within the limits of their resources and within the limits of the present statute, the director and his staff are doing a remarkably good job. Those who are not aware of the extent of activity in this field would do well to read the latest annual report of the director of investigation and research which I tabled in this house on October 15 last.
Perhaps I should remind the house that the director of investigation and research is in a very real sense the watchdog of parliament and the public in the matter of competition policy. He has a statutory duty to undertake an inquiry whenever he has reason to believe that the Combines Investigation Act has been, or is about to be, violated. In this role he has a high degree of independence.
If there are hon. members who feel that the resources of the branch are inadequate, I would have to agree. I would have to say the same about some of the other branches in my department, and no doubt most other ministers would feel the same about the resources available for some of their programs. As a member of the government I support fully the severe measures that have had to be adopted to limit the growth of government expenditure, but we have to recognize that these economies cannot be achieved without some cost in terms of the services we can offer to the Canadian people.
We do not find in the Canadian market, or in any other market, one category of companies that are absolute monopolies, with all the rest operating under conditions of perfect competition. The vast majority of businesses in Canada are found between these two extremes. They operate in varying degrees of

monopolistic competition from one end of the spectrum to the other. While perfect competition may be the ideal, it is rarely attained in practice outside of certain commodity markets where the numbers of buyers and sellers are very large. Our objective has to be to maintain workably competitive situations, to prevent price-fixing and other forms of collusion, and to prevent unfair trading practices likely to reduce the degree of competition by driving firms out of the market.
The fact that many of our manufacturing industries consist of a small number of dominant firms often means that there is a pattern of price leaders and price followers. The price leader establishes a new price and the others follow. Sometimes this takes place within a matter of days or even hours. This does not necessarily mean that there is collusion. The combines staff watch all such situations carefully and consider them against the background of the particular industry as they know it.
A common criticism of the Combines Investigation Act is that it stands in the way of mergers or other arrangements that could lead to increased efficiency through economies of large scale production. This matter is not so simple as some critics imply. An important question is whether in each case the benefits of increased efficiency will be passed on to the public.
Another question is whether the firm concerned is in fact operating at less than the optimum scale. There is a good deal of loose talk about scale in the absence of evidence as to the ideal scale for a particular industry. Fortunately we are beginning to see an increasing flow of economic studies of scale and specialization in Canadian industry, stimulated by the work of the Economic Council of Canada on this subject. Under the present act, when the director examines a merger he is obliged to consider whether competition is, or is likely to be, lessened "to the detriment or against the interests of the public." In his annual reports the director has outlined a number of economic factors and questions he takes into account. These demonstrate that he does not limit himself to a narrow legalistic approach. Moreover, he is always prepared to listen to any proposals and give his opinion as to whether a particular course of action would be likely to necessitate an inquiry under the act.
I hope no one will take these remarks to reflect complacency about the present state of
November 8, 1968

the law. Competition needs to be enforced more effectively in Canada, and the present act is imperfect. Its coverage is not broad enough; many important services are outside its ambit. Based as it is on criminal law, it involves elaborate and lengthy court procedures with a heavy burden of proof resting on the crown. When a case is tried the court must either find that there is a criminal offence or else acquit the accused. The court is not entitled, nor qualified, to temper justice with a judgment about the economic impact of a restrictive practice on the community. The problem of dealing realistically with mergers is related in part to this element of rigidity. Needless to say, my officials and 1 have our own views about a number of ways in which the act should be improved. We are awaiting with interest the report of the Economic Council of Canada on this subject. We hope and expect it will deal constructively with the areas of weakness in the present act. I am in any case determined to propose a series of major reforms in this legislation after we receive the council's report.
Another major influence on competition and efficiency in Canadian industry is the tariff. Tariff reduction is one of the economic remedies provided in the Combines Investigation Act. Historically our relatively high protective tariff contributed to many of the weaknesses that still exist in our manufacturing industries. It encouraged the development of a branch-plant pattern in manufacturing, with the Canadian plant typically emulating its parent by attempting to produce a full range of that company's products. The inevitable outcome has been too many small scale operations and unduly high costs. There is a good deal of evidence that the height of the tariff has also contributed to the emergence of monopolistic conditions in Canadian industry. It is clear that the use of the Combines Investigation Act to enforce competition has to be related to and supported by complementary tariff policies.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
The subjects I have touched upon today, Mr. Speaker, are all interrelated. They are by no means the only factors that affect our competitive position and our price performance. Many other policies must also come into the picture-our programs for manpower training and mobility, our grants to encourage research and development, for example. The house is familiar with these and I do not propose to review them. I have concentrated
The Budget-Mr. Woolliams on two main elements, price stability and competition policy. The main point I want to make is that we must not only do what we can to encourage restraint in regard to increases in prices and costs we must also ensure consistent and vigorous use of all programs that can contribute to a more dynamic, competitive and efficient economy.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the budget debate I intend to deal positively in an approach to one of our major industries in western Canada. Before doing so I should like to comment on a question I asked this morning. I feel that it would be expedient for me to do so at this time. I have in mind the answer of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) in reference to medicare.
We in this house remember when the Liberal party brought in their medicare program. We well remember that at that time Miss LaMarsh said it would be something like the castor oil treatment: open your mouth, you are going to get the treatment whether you like it or not. We were under the impression at that time, rightly or wrongly, that the federal government would pay 50 per cent of the cost and 50 per cent of the cost would be paid by the provinces. Even on that basis I raised an objection because I have always taken the position that the government of Canada cannot legislate programs and thrust them on the provinces, particularly when the province must pay 50 per cent of the cost. The situation is even worse when the federal government turns around and not only requires the provinces to pay their 50 per cent of the cost but also the other 50 per cent.
The new formula announced at the conference between the federal and provincial governments was a real shocker. The federal government probably had it in mind all the time. We are now informed that the federal government intends to opt out of this program. At one time the provinces used to opt out, but on this occasion the federal government is opting out. It has handed the provinces a package and the provinces are not only going to have to pay their 50 per cent but the federal government's 50 per cent. The minister said this earlier in a sophisticated manner. This supports my feeling that we should always accept his words as having two meanings.
Having regard to the 2 per cent tax, or whatever it may be, in relation to medicare, the minister has said that he will look at it to
November 8, 1968

The Budget-Mr. Woolliams see that whatever the government's share of the cost is it will be passed on in the form of revenue to the provinces. What he is really saying is that he will probably take 17 per cent or 20 per cent of the tax collected for this particular purpose and suggest that is the allowance for the provinces and if they cannot live within that amount they will have to put up the balance.
The minister shakes his head. I want the record to show that he has shaken his head because I know the provinces are shaking in their boots and provincial treasurers throughout the country are very worried about this plan. It is too bad but I think the time may come-I do not encourage this-when the provinces will join together and say to the federal government, we are not going to accept this type of plan. The federal government is now thrusting a plan upon them much like the plan that was thrust on them in relation to property and civil rights which are under their jurisdiction. The government said it would pick up the tab for 50 per cent but it now says that the provinces must handle the whole thing and pay 100 per cent. That is not good enough, and it is not acceptable just because the Minister of Finance was not able to calculate within reason how he would manage a balanced budget.
I should like to hear from him on this point at some time. Perhaps he will give us an explanation, assuring the provinces. He may shake his head, but I hope he will say categorically without any of these sophistical reservations that the federal government will pay 50 per cent of the cost and will not come crying here about it being the cause of deficits. Surely he cannot blame the provinces for this fact when it is the government's own grandiose scheme that is responsible.
Before I comment about the petroleum industry I should like to say I listened with great interest to one of the most able lectures that has been delivered outside a law school, that delivered by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford). It was just a lecture and it was read quietly. He broke the frozen silence of his department and gave us a summary of what has been put under one roof. The minister knows that this department has had no effect in controlling the cost of living in this nation. Nor did he indicate any solution his department or any other department has in relation to controlling costs, whether they are the result of high interest rates or high costs of living.

In any event these high costs are having a serious effect on the old age pensioners and others who are tied to that type of income today. The government has forgotten these people; they are the forgotten people. I cannot remember what the increase is in relation to the increased cost of living that these pensioners are allowed, but the minister certainly knows that the old age pensioner today is chained to an economic system within which he cannot live.
We have heard a great deal about poverty in Biafra. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) is at this time conducting a task force tour across the nation. He must be receiving many shocks as a result of the poverty which exists in Canada. The people who are existing in poverty, living in low class housing and suffering this terrible and horrible standard of living, are the old age pensioners, our senior citizens, who are chained to the inflationary economic programs of the government.
The minister can talk as much as he wants about his sources of revenue, but he is perhaps forgetting a most important principle. If you increase trade you increase demand, and when you increase demand you obtain greater supply because production can accelerate. In this way you obtain greater revenue and do not have to bring in a high taxation system. That was the philosophy of this government during the election campaign. Many of the candidates said the government was going to pay as it goes. What they really meant was that the people of Canada would pay and the government would go. That is really the government's philosophy.

That may be true. I have made reference earlier to the grain industry. We warned this government for months about what was happening to grain trade. The government just sat in silence. The minister is now leaving. Of course he must leave, because he cannot stand the heat. Whenever it gets hot he has to get out of the chamber.
Canada is an anomally in the world today. We are currently producing over 200 per cent of its consumption of crude petroleum; yet we have a net deficit in this country of over $200 million per year. There is need for a new oil policy, and that need is essential. Let me pause here for a moment to indicate that in 1960
November 8, 1968	COMMONS
and 1961 the government of that day established a national oil policy. There has not been any change since that time. The circumstances have changed and economies have changed not only in Canada-I have in mind development, consumption and other factors -but throughout the world. This government leans on the fact that we have a national oil policy, but it never really admits it was the government of this party that implemented that policy. That policy now requires upgrading and change.
On October 1, I directed a question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Green) regarding oil policy. I asked him whether there had been a cut-back and he said, as reported at page 625 of Hansard:
-the national oil policy is a matter of continuing negotiation-
There is no question in my mind that there has been a unilateral decision by the United States in reference to cut-backs on the importation of crude petroleum from Canada. This government will not admit that there were no negotiations or no attempt on their part to negotiate.
In this regard I should like to read the following from the Calgary Herald of September 28, 1968:

United States action which could cost Alberta export sales totalling close to ten million barrels of crude oil in the next three months, has created new tensions in Ottawa, Washington and the oil centres of North America.
U.S. companies which import Canadian crude have been "requested" by the U.S. oil import administration to cut back their purchases during the fourth quarter of 1968-
The United States made the request; Canada danced to their tune. There has been no suggestion anywhere, either in the answers to questions by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) or the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene), that there have been any negotiations with the United States, and there has been no suggestion of any protest to that country in respect of the cut-back in our exports of crude petroleum. Bonner H. This was stated before the conservation board in the city of Calgary; yet when I asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce about it I was given the wishy-washy answer that it has always been subject to negotiation under the national oil policy. The fact is that the government never negotiated in this respect and has never protested what has occurred. It has just stood back and lost the petroleum market, in the same way as it stood back and lost the grain market for western Canada. And these are both billion dollar industries.
I have never been one to stand in my place and criticize without offering a solution. We need a new, dynamic oil policy now. We need a policy that takes into consideration recent developments in the industry and changes that can be expected in the future. What is the situation today? We have a problem in the Near East which affects the oil supply of the world. We see scientific development taking place with respect to the Alberta tar sands. We see a tremendous development taking place in Alaska. Yet no consideration is given by the government to the situation that exists, and it has nothing to say about how the problem can be solved. All we have had is a stupid lecture given by the minister-I have used an adjective I should not have used-such as is given in law school.
The minister talks about controlling prices but he offers no solutions to the problem. We are given quiet little lectures which are written by quiet little people in the department. This is the kind of speech to which we have been subjected. We must increase our exports in this area before we can arrive at any solution to the problem. The average daily production for 1967 was 1,098,000 barrels. The average daily consumption during 1967 was
1.294.000	barrels. At the end of 1967 the estimated potential productive capacity was
2.650.000	barrels per day. During 1967 Canada imported an average of 200,000 barrels per day more crude oil and products than it exported. At an approximate laid down price of $2.90 per barrel, this contributed a net annual deficit of approximately $200 million to Canada's trade imbalance. For every thousand barrels per day of Canadian crude produced and sold, there is an approximate saving of $1 million per year in the trade deficit.
If the $200 million were spent in Canada for Canadian crude oil it would have a total effect on the Canadian economy, through
November 8, 1968

The Budget-Mr. Woolliams secondary and tertiary industries, of approximately $700 million annually. Therefore we would increase the gross national product and obtain more tax revenue. Instead of increasing rates, we could have a bigger share of the market and keep the rates at the same level. As I have said, if the $200 million for imports were spent in Canada for Canadian crude oil, it would have a total effect on the Canadian economy, through secondary and tertiary industries, of approximately $700 million annually.
Two major Canadian banking institutions have calculated that the multiplier effect of money generated in the natural resources sector of our economy is approximately 3.3. Canada loses on every barrel of imported crude oil, not only through the foreign production profits that remain offshore but mainly because each barrel of Canadian crude oil pays over $1 per barrel in the form of taxes and payments to the Canadian government. Therefore, to the extent of Canada's crude oil imports payments are received in foreign countries, and if these imports were replaced by Canadian oil it would result in such benefits being received directly by the citizens of Canada. This industry would go a long way to make up our deficits. Canada loses, on the importation of oil, the production costs and $1 in the form of taxes and payments to the Canadian government on every barrel of crude petroleum.
This is the situation. When the national oil policy was developed there were negotiations by the then Conservative government which stepped into the field because at that time, as a result of the Suez crisis, our exports of crude petroleum and other oil products had fallen off. The then minister of trade and commerce, the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees), and others worked out a plan with the United States so that we would export this commodity to the northwest United States and permit crude petroleum to come into this country from Venezuela, which market is financed by American interests. It was agreed that they would have the eastern market and would export to the northeast United States.
As I pointed out to the minister in the late show on October 1, our exports of crude petroleum, have been reduced by at least
10,000	barrels per day because of the unilateral decision of the United States. While their imports into Canada from that country are increasing, our exports to the United States are growing smaller. The Minister of

Finance should walk up and down and think about this situation.
In this connection the government should take a positive step and do something to solve the problem. The government should face the fact that the United States made a unilateral decision in this respect and has cut back our exports. Then it should say: We will send a negotiating team to Washington to arrive at a solution to the problem. The government should send a negotiating team to Washington, rather than sending ministers to South America which means they are never here to answer questions in the house.
The minister should discuss this problem with other members of the cabinet and make certain that our petroleum industry is protected. It is a pretty sad state of affairs if we in Canada cannot protect this most important industry. Even with our exports to the United States, without the cut-back and with the greatest domestic consumption in Canada, our industry is operating today at a production level of only 40 per cent. In other words, we could produce another 60 per cent in this industry and stay within the rules of conservation in the provinces. Now we are bringing into Canada millions of dollars worth of crude petroleum, $200 million a year, which aggravates our balance of trade situation.
What would the grain growers of this country think if we, as a wheat exporting nation, were to import $200 million worth of wheat? I know that the argument put forward is whether we can economically bring the crude or refined petroleum from western Canada into the Montreal area, but the experts point out that we could transport oil to the eastern market and compete with oil coming into this country from Venezuela. If this is true, the government should surely do something to correct the situation, and it should do it now. This should be done, rather than giving wishy-washy answers and trying to sweep the problem under the carpet.
There is nothing wrong, politically, in getting up and saying that the United States has unilaterally cut back our exports and that the government is pleased the opposition has brought the matter to its attention. Then the government should say: We will send a negotiating team to Washington and work out an arrangement. This is the kind of government I thought the Canadian people might be electing under a young man in the last election. However, I have seen no sign of this happening. Mr. Speaker, I hear the hon. member
November 8, 1968

across the way saying something. I do not know what he is muttering about; he is all greased up.
The western Canadian petroleum industry, exclusive of refining and marketing, currently spends approximately $1 billion a year, over 85 per cent of which is spent in Canada, for goods, services and payments to government. Of the major expenditures made for oil and gas pipe lines, gas plants, fittings, pressure vessels, pumps, etc., over 80 per cent was spent in eastern Canada, a large part of which was in the province of Quebec. The majority of these capital expenditures were made in Canada as a result of tariff protection. With that we have no quarrel, because some of our secondary industry needs protection.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
At least 75 per cent of the capital expenditures on the $235 million tar sand plant was spent in Canada, a major portion of which was spent in Quebec. Eighty five per cent of the capital expenditure of a typical western Canadian gas	plant-Homeglen Rimbey,
which costs $18 million-was spent in Canada, of which the substantial portion represented purchases in eastern Canada. So this industry not only means a lot to western Canada, it means a lot to eastern Canada and to the Canadian economy generally.
The royalties paid to Alberta, British Columbia and Saskatchewan benefit Canadian taxpayers in savings to the federal government in federal-provincial equalization payments, in the words of the minister.
Today Saskatchewan is a have province, but only a short time ago it was a have not province. Alberta is a have province. These are have provinces because they have now developed a philosophy with regard to the development of our industries and the increase of our gross national product. It is only then that the nation will have the kind of revenue that it needs so that its citizens can live in dignity, and then perhaps the word "justice" might have some meaning.
What about the taxes received from federal and corporate profits? That in itself is substantial. The direct result of oil, gas and associated mineral development in western Canada has removed both Saskatchewan and Alberta from the provinces currently receiving equalization payments.
The national oil policy resulted in an agreement whereby we would export to the northwestern United States, while we would permit imports of crude from Venezuela. How
The Budget-Mr. Woolliams did this come about? It has come about because, as my good friend knows, in the course of negotiations the United States said: "If we cut off imports of crude petroleum from Venezuela we would be fostering communism in that area and the financial interests of the western world would suffer. If you allow us to import crude petroleum into the eastern market, we will give you markets in western and central United States". So let us follow through the negotiations with the United States. I am not complaining about the United States; they are good, sound businessmen and they will listen to us because Canada is their best customer. This is the plea I make to the government, and it is not made in the form of criticism. It is the kind of positive approach which I thought I would hear in this debate from the government, either with regard to wheat, to industry or to petroleum. However, that is all forgotten.
I suggest the government is permeated with socialistic thinking, so that all they can see are grandiose programs paid by grandiose taxation. What I say may sound like conservatism, but let me say that I listened to a very fine conservative speech from another member from Calgary, the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Mahoney) who spoke last evening, and I want to congratulate him on his maiden speech. I advise everyone to read that speech. I hope that what he said in the house he also said in caucus, but I hope he said it there more forcibly to those ministers who are socializing with socialists.

Mr. Speaker, in the short time that I have left I should like to make several recommendations. The government must get off its butt right now and review the national oil policy, in the light of the changing circumstances which I have mentioned. It should renegotiate a deal with the United States or else tell the United States: Look, you may be worried about Venezuela or about a similar uprising to the one that took place in Peru, and we are also worried about it, but we are concerned about our own economy and we are prepared to allow a certain amount of imports into this country provided you will fulfil the terms of the national oil policy and let us put more into the Toledo, Detroit and Chicago area. I congratulated the government last year when they reversed their previous decision on the pipe line. Now I say they have to renegotiate the national oil policy.
The second recommendation I would make to the government is this. The National Energy Board officials must never be questioned, according to some people. As soon as an administrative board is established in this country, whether it is provincial or federal, it is considered to be a sacred cow. I suggest that the officials of the National Energy Board and the officials of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce should be carefully examined by a standing committee of the House of Commons with regard to what took place between the United States and Canada, and what is taking place now so far as the petroleum industry is concerned, because the ministers will not divulge the facts. I do not know why they do not want to do it.
My third suggestion is that I would like to see the Senate go to work. It should initiate a special economic study of the petroleum industry. It should get experts of all types from the independent petroleum association, from independent companies, from U.S. companies and from the Canadian subsidiaries that may be left. Facts should be set down, after which the committee should come up with a sound basic policy to increase our trade. Why do we need this investigation? We have to find out what effect the new Alaska production has on the national oil policy. The hon. member for Calgary South mentioned it in his speech, and I agree with him 100 per cent. It will have a dynamic effect. These are

DEBATES	November 8, 1968
the factors we must consider, and I am glad the hon. member is in accord with me in that regard. What effect does the Alaska production have on the Puget Sound area, particularly now when the largest cut-backs by the United States are taking place? This is dealt with in the September, 1968 edition of the Calgary Herald.
Will we be able to make up our loss of exports because of the Alaska production, by increasing exports to the Detroit, Toledo and Chicago area? These are the things that should be looked into immediately. A review of the national oil policy is of utmost importance to the economic welfare of Canada, and more important than considering the burdening of the industry with the Carter tax proposals, which sound good in theory and are quoted glibly for vote getting but could and might at this time hamper Canadian production, development and trade expansion. I can never understand those people who talk about taxing Canadian capital, here there and everywhere, these socialist thinkers who are not only on one side of this chamber. We are always talking about U.S. capital. If the government is going to tax Canadians to death, and that is what it is doing, and if it is now going to start taxing capital, because that is what it recommends, it will sap all the capital from Canadians, and how are we ever going to invest in our own country? That is the problem.
I do not know what kind of campaign the Liberals ran across the rest of the country but I have listened to their candidates in Alberta and found them to be the most Goldwater type of people I have ever met. I am not being critical of the hon. member for Calgary South, and I complimented him on his speech, but I thought that if some of these candidates were elected they might have had some power to direct this government into sound business thinking and to cut out the socialist trends which are ruining the welfare schemes, such as medicare which the provinces already had, and imposing a new plan on the provinces which will cost the taxpayers many more thousands of dollars and will sap more capital from Canadians so they will be unable to invest in their own industry. We have had the Watkins report and we have heard Walter Gordon talking about it, but the same people came in with a budget which is taxing capital, so that Canadians do not have the necessary capital to invest in their own industry. I think we need a new policy with regard to the petroleum industry.
November 8, 1968

My time is nearly up but I should like to end on this note. Although trade is most important, it seems to be forgotten today because we are so busy designing plans on taxation. I should like the members of the government to come clean before parliament, so far as the wheat markets of this nation are concerned, because they mean a billion dollars to be spent in the industrial centres of Quebec and Ontario. I hope the government will come clean with the opposition, because it is good government when it does, and that is their function. If the government sat on this side of the house, they would be doing the same thing-trying to get the information out. We want to see where we are going with regard to the petroleum industry.

Instead, they misrepresent the facts, as one of the ministers did back on October 1, when he said there was a cut-back but they were going to negotiate. They were going to meet with the industry itself and work out a plan that would give the industry another 10 per cent. Then we could at least say we had 50 per cent production. These are the two major industries. I do not know where your government is going with the Kennedy round, and other deals that were made. I do not know what impact this is having on industry in eastern Canada, but we hear many repercussions so far as that is concerned. We have never been able to debate that situation; it is always kept quiet.
The situation in those three major areas, wheat, petroleum and the industries of eastern Canada, under that kind of dictation, under that kind of control, with that kind of taxation and that kind of socialization, is that things are stymied and no development is taking place. You know, when you look at your budget, and considering the estate tax situation alone, this is what you find. It is all right to pass on your estate to your widow but, under the government's philosophy, you cannot pass on the estate to your children.
I do not know what the rates of taxation are going to be, and will not know until we get the resolution. However, this is what is going to happen. The small farmer who generally passes the farm on to his son, who in turn passes it on to his son, the little man who means a lot to Canada, is going to find that upon his death the family will have to borrow so much money at Liberal high rates of interest they will have to sell the farm to

We must therefore find new sources of money. In addition, we must bring down the per unit cost of housing by a considerable amount. This can be accomplished in part by standardizing building codes and construction standards across Canada. We must also encourage the use of new building materials. Housing therefore is a matter of social welfare, and the federal government has never failed to show leadership but has, in fact, taken the initiative in practically every housing program. This shows us, Mr. Speaker, that very few people have $10,000 cash. Financial institutions apply the rule that the applicant cannot afford more than 27 per cent of his income for mortgage interest, principal and taxes. This, Mr. Speaker, poses the question: How many families earning $5,000 can afford to save 10 per cent per year, and where can you buy a house in an urban or semi-urban area for $12,500? A man earning $5,000 must pay considerably more than 27 per cent of his income for shelter if he is to live by Canadian standards. He must pay a proportionately

high rent for an apartment or town house, or for a dwelling where they will accept children, or he is driven to buying a more expensive house on a resale basis by taking a second mortgage, with the likelihood of spending 45 to 50 per cent of his income on shelter.
Such mortgage payments and rents, Mr. Speaker, are a major cause of family breakdown because they take the milk from the baby's mouth and shoes from his feet. They deprive him of proper care, and frequently of the loving care of his mother, who often has to work in order to pay the rent or the mortgage.
The problem as far as housing is concerned is how to provide for or accommodate people in the lower income brackets. This problem must be solved by government action, which must be critical of obsolete methods of land assembly, construction and financing. A broad and enlightened attack on the problem is required. The government must not wait until all the contingencies are considered; the time to act is now.
Personally, Mr. Speaker, I regret that action did not begin with this budget, in the form of a land speculation tax on the resale of undeveloped prime land. Such a tax would be a deterrent to persons who buy and sell land without contributing to the development of the country.
I look forward, Mr. Speaker, to the result of the task force under the leadership of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer), which is now studying the problem across Canada. I specifically refer to the policy of the Canadian National Railways of removing the agent operators from certain stations and incorporating these stations into what they refer to as the master agency plan. This is being done under the guise of economy, and is supposed to provide a more efficient service for the user.
I should like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that what the C.N.R. is proposing in these communities is not always in the best interest of

I should like to give you a case in point, Mr. Speaker. The C.N.R. is presently making application to the Canadian Transport Commission to remove the agent operator at Acton, Ontario. If this application is successful it will mean the virtual loss of railway service to this community. Acton is a progressive community of 6,000 people located 40 miles from metropolitan Toronto. I can find no justifiable grounds to abolish railway service in this community, Mr. Speaker. I take strong objection to the cavalier methods used by the C.N.R. prior to making formal application to the board of transport commissioners. It was just over a year ago-on October 13, 1967 to be exact-that Mr. R. T. Vaughan, a vice president of Canadian National Railways, wrote to Dr. Harry Harley, who at that time was federal member of parliament for Halton county, advising him that the first stages of implementation of what the railway call the master agency plan would be put into effect on November 6 of that year.
