Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege for me to have

the opportunity of participating in the consideration of the budget. During those few minutes, I shall try to be as objective as possible, even though some of my remarks or criticisms may not be too agreeable to our friends opposite.
I shall dispense with a full review of the promises and sharp criticisms directed against the ministers in the Diefenbaker government when we were in office, but it is difficult to remain silent about the election campaigns and the destructive criticisms the Liberals directed against the Minister of Finance of that day for showing a deficit in his budget. They promised to the people that as soon as they were in office, the Canadian people would not have any deficit in their budget, that it would be brought back to a more normal size and that, instead of showing deficits, we would have surpluses.
The facts are quite different from the promises made to us during the 1962 and 1963 elections in particular. In fact, since our friends opposite came to power in 1963, they certainly have had plenty of time to implement their promises and to show their ability to manage our country's business. However, today the cost of living is the highest in the whole history of Canada. In fact, according to the most recent statistics, the cost of living reaches 156.6 per cent. This means that a number of small investors and low income citizens have a hard time meeting their expenses at the end of the year.
Furthermore, we are faced with the largest deficit ever known in all our history. At the present time, 4.7 per cent of our labour force is unemployed and, out of this number, 99,000 are in the province of Quebec. Taxes of all kinds are the highest since confederation. The debt per capita is the highest ever known. For the second time in less than a year, personal income tax has been raised. It is the second time that this happens since the Liberals came to power. Postal rates have been increased too and, in some cases, the increase was in the order of 375 per cent.
It is also known that without any previous notice, this government has cancelled the winter works program that enabled municipalities to undertake, during the winter months, very useful works to lessen the evils of unemployment. Is it also to promote the building industry that this government maintains the 12 per cent tax on building materials? On several occasions, we on this side of the house tried to persuade the government of the benefit that would be derived from the removal of this 12 per cent tax, as it
November 8, 1968



would enable small investors to build themselves a home, but every time we ran into objections on the part of government members.
Everybody knows that this government has always encroached upon fields of provincial jurisdiction. This government will not grant the provinces their fair share of the tax revenue. As a result of such a position, Mr. Speaker, there remains a certain mistrust between the parties concerned; the government and the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) should take a new stand.
Mr. Speaker, as I have but little time at my disposal this afternoon, I should like to talk about something that concerns the riding I have the honour to represent in this house, namely the textile industry.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
This is one of the oldest industries in the province of Quebec. In that province, the textile industry provides employment for 52,000 Quebecers. There are plants in all or almost all the cities of the province and it is to be noted that those plants are mostly located in small or medium-sized towns.
This is to say that the textile industry has played along the years a very important part in the economy of our cities. We find a great number of textile workers in towns with a population of 5,000, 10,000 or 25,000 people, and they are the strength of our municipalities. They are home owners, people who have succeeded in saving enough money to build themselves a decent home for their family.
During the years 1960, 1961 and 1962, through the imaginative measures of the then minister of trade and commerce, (Mr. Hees), the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings, the textile industry has taken a new lease on life, whereas it was declining before 1960. Thanks to the measures taken by the minister of trade and commerce at that time, this industry found new foreign markets. We were surely entitled to expect that those would be continued. However, conditions today have forced us to realize that the present situation is exactly the opposite of what it was in 1960-62.
The textile industry is now going through a period of uncertainty which is worrying not only the owners of our textile factories, but even more the workers. Mr. Speaker, those are the results of the unconcern shown by the present government towards the textile industry.
A few weeks ago I had the opportunity of meeting the owner of a textile factory in my
The Budget-Mr. Ricard region who had asked me to his office to discuss the matter.
Since it is always a delicate subject to mention names in the house without being authorized to do so, I asked that plant manager whether he objected to my giving names and figures about his own business. He said: I do not object at all because it is a matter of life or death for my own industry and for that of others also.
That industry is the Yamaska Shirts located in St. Hyacinthe. It has been operating in that city since 1929. Until recently, it had 350 employees on a yearly basis. However, since August last, due to a lack of orders, the management has been compelled to reduce its number of employees by about one half. Should the situation continue there will have to be further cuts in the number of employees according to Mr. Yvon Bolduc, the manager of this firm.
Mr. Speaker, the employees and their families are affected adversely by those conditions which are detrimental also to the well-being of many other Canadians who are entitled to expect from the government more protection than they have been given until now.
If you look for the basic reasons for this lack of work not only in that particular plant but and in many others, you will find that it is due mainly to excessive imports from foreign countries, particularly from communist and Asiatic countries.
I have before me, Mr. Speaker, the findings of a survey by the Canadian Textile Institute which gives not only very interesting information but shows to what extent imports are hurting the Canadian industry.
I would like to quote a few figures from the pamphlet I have in hand.

Recently we learned with great shock that at least four textile plants located in St. Hyacinthe, St. Jean and Coaticook were liquidating, forcing hundreds of employees into astoundingly growing joblessness.

Mr. Speaker, that is the situation in the textile industry.
There is one measure that the government could take; it could protect our workers because according to my information, Canadian tradesmen can get boys' shirts from Thailand at $14.50 a dozen, federal tax included. In Canada it would cost a Canadian manufacturer $26.55 to make a dozen shirts of similar quality. As far as men's shirt are concerned, an importer or a tradesman can get foreign shirts for $18.50, federal tax included, whilst the same product or a similar product manufactured in Canada, will cost him $34.50 a dozen.

It seems to me that the government of Canada has an obligation to give the Canadian workers and taxpayers the protection to which they are entitled and to guarantee that they will be able to continue working in the factories where they gained their experience and where their skills are still needed. If the present trend continues, the textile industry will completely disappear a few years from now, and we will all be sorry to see the end of an industry which, until now, has greatly contributed to the success and development of our municipalities.
It seems to me that the government should adopt anti-dumping legislation which would give our workers the protection they need. In my opinion, this legislation should prevent the entry into Canada of foreign products which compete with Canadian products.
If our Canadian factories can manufacture
24.000	or 30,000 dozen of shirts a year, we should not allow the entry into the country of
24.000	or 30,000 dozens of shirts, or whatever the figure, unless they are appraised at the same price as the shirts manufactured in Canada. That would put Canadian and foreign manufacturers on an equal footing. Unless such steps are taken, I am afraid our industry will sooner or later go bankrupt.
Mr. Speaker, I should now like to make a few comments on the first budget introduced by the Minister of Finance. I do not direct my remarks exclusively to him, because to my mind he is merely the tool of the government. I do not want the minister to think that I am criticizing him personally, but rather the policy he is implementing.
I should like to point out to the hon. minister what same journalists think of his first budget. For instance, I have here an article written by Roland Gagne, which appeared in La Voix de I'Est, on October 25, 1968 in which he gives his impressions on the budget of the hon. minister.
In our opinion, it is an injustice, because it is not the average wage earner, who always gets the beating, but the higher wage earner who has the means to pay higher income tax when the financial situation ol the state requires it. The least that can be said Is that Mr. Benson could have strained his grey matter to a greater extent to find less onerous sources of revenue for the people in the low and moderate Income groups.

Mr. Benson should have taken Into consideration the high cost of living, the ever increasing prices, as well as the difficulties Canadians face daily in trying to make ends meet. Their income is by no means inexhaustible. The income that remains, once taxes have been paid, is barely sufficient to provide them with a decent standard of living.
November 8, 1968

And Mr. Gagne concludes by saying:
Why can the Minister of Finance not be reasonable, why can his tax measures not be fair and equitable for all Canadians?
In an editorial published in the newspaper Le Droit of October 23 last, having concurred with the stand taken by the minister towards insurance companies, Marcel Gingras adds this:
That satisfying measure unfortunately is matched by a mean action which will affect again the small wage earners who are urged to save while invited to subscribe generously to the latest issue of Canada savings bonds. The just society, at that price, becomes extremely expensive and we shall regret having ever wished for it.
Now, here is the opinion of a labour leader whose every day work brings him in continuous contact with the workers who let him know about their needs. This is what Mr. Laberge, president of the Q.F.L. said with regard to the first budget presented by the Minister of Finance and I quote:
-the two per cent increase In personal income tax, with its $120 ceiling, is a real hold-up against low income people by a government which managed fraudulently to be elected on the basis of a just society.

A lot more could be said about this budget, but since the time allotted to me is nearly over, I would simply appeal to the fair-mindedness of the minister and tell him that many today are the citizens who got fooled by the promise of a just society as proposed by this government.

Mr. Speaker, I know it is traditional for a member speaking for the first time in the house to say a few words about his constituency. I would not wish to break with such a tradition.
York Simcoe is a new constituency, I am a new member, and I am relatively new to the area I represent. It is now my home and I have come to know it well. Those members who have visited York Simcoe know that it is a rural area lying between Barrie and Toronto. They will also know that it contains some of the loveliest land in Canada, from rolling hills to the Holland Marsh. They should know something of its roots in our history; the Scottish and British settlers and the French speaking pioneers, and the Quakers who first inhabited the area. Hon. members will know that more recently it has attracted people from many lands, who have also made their contribution. Its people are warm and hospitable, and it is an honour for me to have been accepted by them, as well as a privilege to represent these Canadians in the House of Commons.
In some ways my previous experience might have led me to attempt to enter political life. As a university teacher of political science I knew the frustration of lecturing about political problems without having to do anything about them. When I entered public service, first as a diplomat, and later as a ministerial assistant, I had some opportunity to deal with the problems facing this country. But I doubt that I would have attempted political office had it not been for the personality and the policies of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
2610	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Roberts
The concept of government, which the Prime Minister espouses, which seeks the active participation of the public in decisions which affect them

a government of involvement-is a vision of Canada which attracts me. This led me to enter public life to give what support I could to the person who I believe understands best the country that, ideally, Canada can be.
Today I should like to speak on the problems and prospects which face regional development in this country. It has become clear that Canada is moving out of an era of welfare politics into a period in which a primary concern will be the programs and politics of economic development. The whole emphasis on the implementation of welfare programs since the second world war-the establishment of a national system of social security- useful and important as these programs have been, has not moved us very far in eradicating the disparities of regional development which exist in this country. After a century of growth almost one quarter of our families in Canada are living at or under the poverty level.
Our past programs have treated the symptoms of poverty rather than the disease. The key to combatting the poverty problem is the channelling of more funds to realize the untapped potential of underdeveloped regions of our country. Their function must not be to provide a permanent crutch, or support, for lagging sectors, but to give temporary infusions of capital which will bring these regions to a level at which they can sustain their own growth and contribute to our national prosperity.
The proposed department of regional development will fail in this task unless it is conceived, not simply as a department of regional development but as a department which is concerned with general economic planning for the whole of Canada. Such a role opens up a whole nest of problems both within the structure of federalism and within the framework of interdepartmental relations within the government. The department of regional development, if it is to succeed, must take on this larger role simply because of the extent of interdependence within our society and our economy.
The whole history of the rural development program, for instance the agricultural and rural development administration, and the fund for rural economic development, is instructive from this point of view. ARDA was originally conceived as a program to deal

DEBATES	November 8, 1968
with specific, ad hoc, one shot agricultural programs. An analysis soon indicated that over half the people living in rural areas were not engaged in agriculture. As a result, a program directed simply toward agricultural problems could not deal with the underdevelopment of rural areas. The emphasis of programs shifted from agricultural projects to general projects in rural areas. We then found that even concentration on individual and specific projects was not enough. We cannot rely upon piecemeal plans. You have to look for programs in rural areas as a whole. Therefore we moved to a comprehensive development approach, and this led us to the creation of the $300 million FRED.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
At the same time we found that one basic problem in lagging areas was the lack of potential employment opportunities. Consequently, the programs which were designed to improve labour mobility and enhance occupational skills have necessarily resulted in the migration of people from rural to urban areas. We were in danger of solving the problems of rural areas simply by compounding the problems of urban areas. So in the rural development program we have been led step by step to the necessity of regional economic development because we have found that development problems cannot be efficiently dealt with outside this framework.
I suggest that regional economic planning does not make much sense unless it is related to some over-all conception of economic objectives for the country as a whole. Only through such a conception can one keep regional developments operating harmoniously with each other rather than at cross purposes. But of course there are enormous problems in developing a useful system of economic planning in Canada, problems posed by the nature of federalism, by our economic traditions and by our strong interdependence as a trading nation within the North American economy.
Obviously whatever economic planning we have, it must involve close co-operation with the provincial and municipal governments. But one danger of this co-operation may be to remove the planning process from the effective scrutiny of the political process. Planning agreements hammered out in consultation with the provinces would become rigid documents. The House of Commons on the one hand, and the provincial legislatures on the other, will be told that nothing can be
November 8. 1968

changed since changes would restart the whole process of consultation and negotiation. In other words, there is a real danger that planning for regional development will become, in an exact literal sense, an irresponsible process. Positions will be taken with the provinces by planners and technocrats. For parliaments and legislatures to bring effective scrutiny and control to such a process will be extremely difficult.
We have seen how difficult it is for the public to ascertain governmental responsibility for the implementation of shared cost programs with the provinces. Indeed, the fudging of the lines of responsibility is one reason they are brought into discredit. Many members of this house have indicated their concern at the erosion of parliamentary control which has resulted from delegated legislation. There is a real danger that planning decisions, too, will, in effect, be delegated to organs of federal and provincial co-operation which it will be difficult for the House to control.
The process of planning is not simply a technocratic function. Any planning process, since it allocates scarce resources, involves a choice of means and ends which embody political preferences. Through planning certain groups are helped and encouraged, others are limited in their activity. We cannot avoid political judgments in this process.
It is for this reason that I am hopeful the minister responsible for regional development will engage the parliamentary committee fully in the regional planning process. Political choices-I am not speaking of partisan politics must inform technocratic judgment.
A second important factor will be the engagement of the people to be affected by planning, in the planning process. The French have had considerable success in this "animation sociale" and it might be that we could well adapt their use of regional and sector commissions to involve labour, industry, consumers, experts and others in the planning process. This public involvement is vital if planning is to succeed. People must be consulted and their judgments must carry weight.
The French government achieves this through 23 sector commissions. These commissions work on preliminary growth estimates prepared in a five-year basis by the "Commissariat au Plan". Since the commission include representatives of administration, business leaders, experts, people from universities and wage earners, they are able
29180-165j
The Budget-Mr. Roberts to thrash out different opinions and obtain wide agreement on development prospects. The process both overcomes the isolation of government departments, which tend to work in water-tight compartments, and engages public support for planning objectives. We in Canada have to go further, I believe, in involving the parliamentary committee in this kind of work.
Administrators like a quiet life. Civil servants involved in regional planning are not exempt from this general principle. Yet the objective of social participation in planning is to make their life unquiet. It is to ensure that the results of the planning process really do embody a consensus of the views of the groups affected by change. I hope that the minister responsible for this department will ensure that his civil servants will lead unquiet lives in this regard.
The second major problem area for a department of economic development is that of interdepartmental relations.
In most countries-Great Britain and France are good examples-the government departments responsible for economic development sooner or later run headlong into the policies of ministries of finance. The concern of ministers of finance is, after all, fiscal policy and their immediate concern is the short term view of the next 12 months. The view of economic planners is on the five, 10 or 20 year scale. In government, as we know, the urgent often takes precedence over the important. The problem is how to ensure that the planning voice is heard strongly in government councils which are markedly oriented to immediate budgetary and fiscal concerns. To attach economic planning responsibility to the head of government precludes the kind of attention the planning process requires. To attach it to the Department of Finance is to entrust a tender child to a notorious cannibal.
The best solution would appear to be to attach it to a strong minister with easy and influential access to the head of government. This I hope, and I am sure, happily, is the situation now in Canada. What is also required is to make budget making open to the increasing need of public involvement with the budgeting process. A whole mythology surrounds the present budgetary process. A delicious sense of mystery tantalizes those who wonder what the Minister of Finance will do. Obviously some economic decisions being considered by a government cannot be
2612	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Roberts discussed publicly, since public discussion would in itself have the effect of limiting the government's free decision. Devaluation is a perfect example.
But I believe it would be useful to have in a general way more information than we now receive in respect of the various economic measures the government is considering. The United States, for instance, is able to discuss budgetary proposals in congressional committees without an enormously disruptive effect. It seems to me that we possibly might be able to do the same thing.
At the moment, advice which is too narrowly channelled through one small group of people-and this is what happens at the present time-no matter how able those people are, is likely to prove inadequate. This is one reason I welcome the announcement of the recent appointment of an economic adviser to the Prime Minister, and I hope that one of his jobs will be to provide an assessment of Canada's economic policy apart from the views of the Department of Finance.
It would also be helpful if the forecasting services of the Department of Finance were improved, and eventually that the government reveal the long term forecasts on which it is working. These forecasts should be treated not as fixed goals which it is the determination of a government to achieve; they should be looked at as "best estimates," and it should be recognized that policies will change as circumstances change and as estimates prove to be more accurate. Such forecasts and policies tentatively framed in relation to them, will give us a much better assessment of a government's performance. At the moment it is too easy to justify economic success and failure as a result of the imponderable factors in unrealized forecasts.
Regardless of the difficulties of the forecasting process, government must obviously come to some view of what the performance of the economy is likely to be over a five-year period as a context for the yearly budgetary program. Indeed, in terms of the allocation of governmental program priorities the government must look at the life of a parliament as a planning period. Government program priorities are linked to budgetary allocation. A budget can only properly be assessed when viewed in the context of the longer period of government legislation and spending plans. I very much hope that the Minister of Finance will take steps-perhaps others than those I have suggested-to open up the budgetary

Mr. Speaker, as I speak in this house for the first time, I should like to address a few words to my French Canadian colleagues.
I must say that my concept of Canada is that of a country founded on the equalitarian principles of North America, a country with two languages, two cultures, rich from a material point of view, richer still from the spiritual point of view.
I am convinced that such a concept of our country requires the full participation of French Canada. I wish French Canada the role of an equal partner in the management of this country, and French Canadians actual and not merely symbolical power in the management of governmental, administrative and economic affairs of our country.
To all the members, on both sides of the house, I want to say that I am extremely proud to be their colleague, to sit with them, to have the honour of participating, even in a minor capacity, in the management of the affairs of our country.

Mr. Speaker, I respectfully request your tolerance and understanding in bearing with me during my first speech in the house. Indeed, while to me it must be a very important phase of my political life, I realize only too well that to you it is but one of many speeches you have heard in your illustrious term of office.
I hope too, Mr. Speaker, that all members of the house will bear with me in what I have to say, as I know that every one of the 264 members who occupy seats here in this chamber have been or will be charged with the duty and honour of giving his first speech in the House of Commons.
It is with a great sense of pride and humility that I stand here and with a weight of responsibility in the knowledge that I represent over 70,000 men, women and children in the riding of Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe in the province of Newfoundland. But I realize too, Mr. Speaker, that whilst my immediate duty is to my constituents, I am also responsible to the half million people of my province and indeed to the many millions of Canadians across our great dominion.
November 8, 1968

I hope that I may be forgiven if I do not deal specifically with the issue at hand, that is the budget, but what I intend to do is to deal generally with the spending of moneys, as it applies to the nation, by the federal government, and its application in its contributions to the province which I represent, together with my six other colleagues.
If I am critical, it is with respect to those I criticize, not for the sake of criticism alone. I wish to point out what I believe have been very grave errors of judgment, and I hope that some of the criticisms will leave a small mark of recognition on those who are responsible for spending, so that these errors will not be repeated in the future, to bring about the suffering of those who can least afford to suffer.
Due to my somewhat modest military background, in assessing the capabilities of the present government I cannot for the life of me understand their approach to the administration of our country, and I was immediately struck with the fancy military cliches reflected in the government's plan of operation. I refer to cliches like the war on poverty, task forces, training and mobility, strategy, and many other military terms. I would not be surprised if any day now we were to see a platoon of 29 ministers march into the house in the new green uniforms. If indeed the government intends to use military strategy in their attack on the country's problems, may I remind them of the fundamental military term, "appreciation of the situation". May I also remind them of such fundamental terms, which they seem to have forgotten, as basic training, common sense, sincerity, fundamental planning, and the important term, leadership.
With the change in the high command, they have started a change in departments. Let me remind them that if they are going to start playing soldier they are not going to fight the war on poverty by creating new departments. They are not going to overcome neglect, regional disparity, unemployment or the lack of housing by attacking these problems with task forces or by overstaffing their offices with research experts, psychologists or sociologists, by computers, or by looking at maps or reading statistics. They can only find the solutions by using their basic training knowledge or by looking over the ground.
You cannot solve the problem of housing in Newfoundland by sending task forces to the
The Budget-Mr. Marshall capital of the province and asking questions of the very people who caused the problem, that is the provincial government. You can only solve the problem by visiting the village, the settlement, the town or the community where the problem exists, and has existed for 20 years, due to ineptitude and political waste. You cannot talk training and mobility to Newfoundlanders who have been deprived of an education, due to apathy and complacency of government. You cannot talk centralization and reorganization to people who have been discriminated against, and who have never been afforded the common everyday basic services which should be their basic right. You cannot solve problems by thinkers' conferences and seminars and by preparing fancy reports; you can only solve them by getting to the grass roots of the problem and using a bit of common sense. You can only solve them by getting your hands a little dirty and your feet a little wet.
No, Mr. Speaker, our government has created a Frankenstein and has become so absorbed in creating royal commissions to tackle problems, royal commissions which after years of time and millions of dollars only tell them in the end what they knew when they started, that there is a problem. And nine times out of ten the government disregards the report, anyway.
I like the report on poverty of the Economic Council of Canada. After hundreds of pages, five annual reviews, 32 staff studies, five conferences, after presenting seven papers and nine other reports, they came up with the statement that poverty is real. What a stroke of genius! Is there anybody in this house, in the press gallery or in the visitors gallery who did not know that poverty is real? Do not the five million poverty stricken Canadians know that poverty is real?
I liked reading a couple of months ago of the grand celebration the government had here in Ottawa when, with great fanfare and publicity, the Prime Minister by the mere pressing of a button launched a new machine that tells us how many children are born each day. How much did this wonderful invention cost? But let me suggest to the government that they invent some new attachments for that machine which will tell them what happens to the babies born in depressed areas who will be deprived of an education. Let them find an attachment that will tell them what happens to those children who grow up without an education and cannot find jobs. Let them attach something to this machine to

The Budget-Mr. Marshall prepare these babies for the neglect they will find in the fishing settlements of Newfoundland, where people do not have such bare necessities as water and sewerage, lights and telephones, doctors and nurses. Let the machine tell these babies how they can learn to understand the look of disillusionment and despair in the faces of their parents, when they are old enough to understand.
What is the purpose of all these royal commissions? Let us consider first the commission on the status of women. Why are thousands of dollars wasted to investigate the status of women? Why the waste of time and money when everyone in the country knows that any woman can become anything a man can aspire to become? Are there not women doctors, lawyers, professors, scientists and mayors? Are there not women members of parliament and senators who help govern the country? I would even go farther and admit that women can achieve what no man can: They can produce the children that we hope will grow up to become better clothed and fed and educated, and to become better leaders of our country. But let them also be reminded that they are mothers and that they should bring up our children by example and, before it is too late, prevent the diseases that are infesting our youth with glue sniffing, hippie-ism and rioting which I feel is getting out of hand and, if we are not careful, will result in the decay of our youth of the future.
Here we are in a state of financial chaos. The other day I read in Time magazine about the general and his lieutenants going off on junkets to Latin American countries. They are going on a month long mission to Latin America, on a belated voyage of exploration, to look into the all important aspects of our relations with Venezuela, Colombia, Peru, Chile, Argentina and Brazil, and other Latin American countries. They are going to have a shuttle service between Ottawa and Latin America.
Did anyone ever hear of anything so absurd? They are making a mess of running their own country and here they go looking for trouble in other countries. They cannot solve their own basic problems and they go looking for new ones. I say to them in all sincerity, let us clean out our own backyard before we go trying to solve someone else's problems. If the Prime Minister wants to go on a voyage of exploration, let me take him on a voyage to my district in Newfoundland to look into the all important relations with

the most neglected part of Canada. I will take his cabinet on a voyage which win make them hang their heads in shame.

Leave the people of Canada alone, I say. We have lived together in unity for 100 years by applying the common sense laws created by the Fathers of Confederation. National unity will result from the feeling we have in our hearts, the way we help our neighbours, regardless of race, creed or colour. We had examples of this during world war II, Mr. Speaker. No one told the French, the Italians, the Ukrainians, the Jews or the many other nationalities that they had to fight for Canada against German tyranny. They did so because they were Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal for a few moments with regional disparities in Canada. This gay cavalier that we have for a finance minister shrugged his shoulders and made casual references to disparities among the provinces when he introduced his budget. It did not seem to matter whether these disparities were social, geographic or occupational. He did not offer the germ of an idea for solving the problems of some of the people in this country. He treated Canada as if its population were members of a large affluent club. This club, Mr. Speaker, had suffered some additional expenses, so the minister had decided to raise the dues. It did not matter that these dues fell a little hard on some people. I would suggest to the minister that these dues were particularly unfair to some people who cannot ever hope to become members of this club. The budget should have had some solutions to put forward for those who are faced with problems.
I should like to deal briefly, Mr. Speaker, with the problem facing our fisheries. For 20 years all our fishermen have heard are excuses; their problems still remain to be solved. It does not matter whether these problems relate to freshwater or saltwater fishing. Government solutions have in fact been inept and the budget contains no fresh ideas for tackling these problems. Certainly there have been no ideas on the part of the Department of Fisheries. I suggest that if an official in the Department of Fisheries were given an order book and told to go out and get orders for fish, he would not know what to do with the book. It is high time the government and the Department of Fisheries took the initiative and acted imaginatively to solve the problems facing our fishermen in Canada, whether those problems be geographic or occupational.
For example, Mr. Speaker, the fishing industry needs a Colonel Sanders to do for fish what he has done for chicken. I think it is high time we took a different look at our problems from the one taken hitherto.
Let me give another example, Mr. Speaker, which is really an association of words. If a housewife sees a newspaper headline that
November 8, 1968
reads: "New government budget has a fishy look", and she goes to market, naturally she will not buy any fish; she will probably buy beef or chicken or some other foodstuff. The businessman, already worried about increased taxation, is not going to eat fish when he goes to a restaurant; he will eat something else.
The hon. member for Surrey (Mr. Mather) had a good idea, Mr. Speaker, and I should just like to quote from a newspaper report I have which set forward this idea:
Instead of "fish", Barry Mather has tipped Jack Davis, sell it with some "flair and imagination- give it a little supermarket sex appeal."
Call it anything, says Barry Mather, but don't call it "fish".
Call it what it is: Boundary Bay Crab, B.C. Red Spring Salmon, West Coast Cohoe, Gaspe Salmon, New Brunswick Sardines, Nova Scotia Lobster, Athabaska Salmon Trout-
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that what is required here is a different approach. In effect, we should use modern methods of merchandizing in the fisheries. Fish should be advertised as something that people want to eat. Salesmen in the Department of Fisheries should actually think, eat, sleep and dream fish. They should advertise this commodity so that people want to eat it. Therefore what is required is imagination and initiative, and it is time that something was done.
May I now turn for a moment, Mr. Speaker, to the grains industry in western Canada. This is a highly efficient industry, or could be made into such, but our grain producer is on the horns of a dilemna. If he spends more money on fertilizers, on new machinery or on improving the production of grain, he only adds to the surplus problem now facing our farmers. If he enlarges his input of money and output of production, and then finds he cannot sell that production, then all he is left with are "put-puts" and no money.
Last year, Mr. Speaker, since the international grains agreement had expired the government lost sales to Japan and other countries. The United States and France took them away from us. The government woke up too late, realized that the market had gone, and our farmers now have a surplus of grain on their hands. For all that the Canadian government has done to sell grain, Mr. Speaker, you might suppose that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) were praying for drought in China. The situation was bad enough last year; this year there is an additional surplus on the prairies. What are the government doing about it now?
2617
The Budget-Mr. Rod Thomson
We lost some sales last year, Mr. Speaker, and I suggest that we are going to lose more this year unless our Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce gets busy and shows some imagination and initiative in this area as well. We have sent abroad salesmen from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce who admittedly have sold a lot of wheat. These people deal with governments and with international trading agreements, and that is fine. But what have they or the government done to sell wheat in the modern merchandizing sense?
Let me give another example, Mr. Speaker. I have been told that the people of India and some other Asian countries do not have a taste for wheat or wheat products in the sense that we in the western world have. Perhaps this product should be prepared in some other way in which they would eat it. For instance, corn could be turned into corn syrup or corn liquor. We might have to use different methods of preparing wheat for sale.
I should also like to suggest that to promote trade with these people we change the form of a product. Let us look for what the market demands, not at what we have for sale. We might also do a little research in other countries and be able to show them whether it is economical for them to buy wheat or to sell rice, or whether it is in their interest to purchase a high protein grain which could be used to more advantage in their country. I doubt whether we have done much in this area. We should actually search the market for ways to enlarge the sale of our products.
We in western Canada, Mr. Speaker, realize that you cannot hope always to sell the total crop that you have on hand. We must be prepared as farmers to carry some stocks in our own granaries as part of our business, if you like. Grain is a important commodity to Canada, and as a nation we might well consider establishing a national food bank, call it a strategic reserve, or what you will.
We might also explore the possibility of selling grain to the sterling areas, or to the Japanese, taking Japanese yen or sterling in return. I will give the house an illustration of what I have in mind. If we were to sell 100 million bushels of wheat, roughly $200 million worth, to Japan and we took the equivalent in yen, then the wheat could be paid for by using some of our supply of gold or U.S. dollars that we have on hand. We could pay the farmers out of this money, and it would not cost the Canadian taxpayer a cent. Admittedly, Mr. Speaker, it might reduce our

If we were wise we would spread our trade among several countries. This is particularly so in view of the internal problems in the United States, with whom a large proportion of our business is done.
Very soon, Mr. Speaker, the Japanese will be holding a world trade fair. What better way could we honour them than by selling to them some of our products, taking yen in return? I have a yen to go to Japan to see that trade fair, and I should like some yen on hand to pay my way when I get there.

I should like to deal for a few moments with the effects agriculture has on the economy of Canada as a whole. Agriculture accounts, I think, for approximately 7 per cent of the gross national product, but believe me there are some sections of the economy which have a great deal more influence on the rest than dollars would suggest. Back in the 'fifties when we had a national surplus of wheat, the first industries in the east which felt the impact were those which were related to western agriculture

industries manufacturing farm machinery and the like. One week end when I was home I went around and asked a number of businessmen what the situation was, at that time, as far as business was concerned. They said: It has been slow this fall and unless larger grain sales are in prospect it will be slower still. When one sees dozens of high priced tractors or combines standing on an implement dealer's lot, it will not be too long before the problem is back in Ontario, or Quebec.
Let me suggest in closing that as we try to solve the problems of our neighbours, as we try to solve the problems of different regions in Canada, we frequently solve other problems as well. But if we are selfish and self-centered, tending to look after a particular area only, the other problems are likely to grow. By helping to solve the problems of other people we can frequently solve our own.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour, as the member for the riding of Lotbiniere, to participate in the debate on the budget which, in this instance, is the first budget brought down by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) in

order to add to what the members of the Ral-liement Creditiste have already said in the house on what we think of the budget and its effects.
Mr. Speaker, our country must reorganize itself in the light of the past and the present. We live in a young country, but after 100 years of attempts, successes and failures, we must lay the foundation for a modern country, keeping what has served it well and improving what has failed.
For several years now, in the face of great difficulties and an alert and alarmed public opinion, our governments set up royal commissions on various topics, which commissions, headed by experts, heard the grievances, collected evidence, accumulated statistics, with a view to delineating each specific problem. In the light of those facts, the commissioners produced recommendations to enlighten our legislators in the heavy responsibility of drafting laws.
For instance, we know of reports equally famous and modernistic, such as the Glassco report on the administration of the government which was intended to make that organization more functional, more streamlined, according to modern standards.
We have had the Carter report on taxation, which aimed at redefining and altering the structure of our obsolete taxation system, tax-sharing formulas, and so on.
We have had-and there is still more to come, for it is not yet completed-the report on bilingualism and biculturalism, which deals with the problem of languages, races, cultures and minorities in Canada with a view to presenting solutions which will allow each individual and the whole Canadian people to develop fully, each according to his own means of expression.
We have had the report on foreign ownership and the structure of the Canadian industry. We have had the report on the Canadian banking system.
Mr. Speaker, we do not necessarily have to support all the recommendations found in each one of those reports. Nevertheless, the fact remains that these studies have been made at great expense to the Canadian people and should be used for a concrete purpose, helping us to build a modern country for a dynamic people.
I am clearly under the impression that those studies which cost millions of dollars of the taxpayers' money were only effected to calm down a storm, to suppress a tendency and to justify the inaction of the government.
November 8, 1968

Private industry, Mr. Speaker, is constantly reviewing its organization, its structures, its means and objects. It is not afraid of development, competition and modernization, otherwise it would run the risk of being left behind.
A private enterprise which would stop developing-as everybody knows and recognizes-could not remain in existence. The same applies, in my opinion, with a few exceptions, to the government.
That is the reason why, it is unthinkable that such serious studies made on such basic subjects should be consigned to oblivion or put off indefinitely.
In the meantime, the government is losing valuable time which could be better used for the progress of Canada. The government is gathering tools, but he remains passive, stagnant. That is not the way to progress, but to lose ground, and the last budget is the best proof of what I am saying. In order to convince ourselves of this, let us scrutinize this famous budget.
A few days ago the Minister of Finance tabled for the information of Parliament the 1968 White Paper on the Canadian economy: review and outlook, and his budget.
It is always an ardous task to read a budget, or a White Paper, because it is highly technical and mathematical. However it always makes for interesting reading since it analyzes a situation which otherwise would be difficult to grasp fully in all its details.
I wish first of all to thank the minister who with the help of his officials has so well depicted the economic situation prevailing in Canada today.
Secondly, I wish to blame him for his lack of solutions to the problems which are at the root of that economic situation.
As in every budget speech-and this one is not any different-no short or long term solution is offered to correct such and such a situation. This is what I regret. In order to find one or more solutions, we must inevitably refer, for instance, to the various reports of the Economic Council of Canada which sets forth the situation in a concise but specific manner, and which puts more emphasis on the solutions.
I shall first refer to the main points of the budget, on which are based the minister's contentions, in order to shed some light on the flagrant contradictions to be found in the present and past administrations.
29180-166J
The Budget-Mr. Fortin
On the one hand, hourly rates of salary keep on increasing and, on the other hand, unemployment keeps increasing. This trend, Mr. Speaker, has been sustained for twenty years or more. The main feature of our modem economy is the gradual taking over of labour by the machines.
Under our present monetary system, the purchasing power is nearly all distributed in the form of wages, salaries and other means of paying for work done in production or distribution firms. Meanwhile, the purchasing power is necessarily reduced, as manual labour is being replaced by machinery and payrolls are cut down, in spite of an increase in production capacity.
Our economy is subjected to tremendous pressures through unavoidable price increases caused by higher salaries. And these are just as unavoidable, as every worker wants naturally and normally more security for himself and his family, because this security is threatened by automation. As a result, what must come is what learned economists call the higher cost of living-higher unemployment relationship.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
When you have a higher cost of living on the one hand, Mr. Speaker, and on the other hand a lower income because the work done by man-not the work done by machines-is reduced, the inevitable mathematical result is more poverty and less buying power. Such is the shame of our economy: "Want in the midst of plenty" as the Creditistes put it.
The former Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) said in the August, 1965 issue of the Labour Gazette, and I quote:
Poverty, wherever it exists, is a threat to everyone's prosperity.
He was right, Mr. Speaker. What a pity that we should be satisfied with just saying so, satisfied with the lure of mere words!
What emerges from this government from the economic viewpoint can be summarized in this very short and accurate expression: "A sea of words, a desert of ideas and achievements".
The guideline of the International Labour Organization set forth by the Minister of Labour of that time must also apply to Canada.
In spite of the fact that most of our fellow citizens are comfortably off, we shall not truly be able to call Canada a prosperous country as long as poverty will exist within its borders. Such poverty, no doubt, exists. In fact, there are people in our country who
November 8. 1968

The Budget-Mr. Fortin have been left behind by progress and who, without assistance, will never get back on their feet. Paradoxically those people can barely survive and the government takes away once more, their purchasing power, under the pretence of social progress, which I fail to understand.
Our governments, for more than a hundred years, have been fooling themselves if they believe as they give evidence of it every day, that an increase in productivity will solve the problem of people being replaced by machines.
It is not a question of protesting against the machine, but rather of making each individual participate in the productivity by giving him his share of production which the machine has developed for him on his behalf.
We have the social responsibility to give the opportunity to each and every one, without exception, of enjoying an honest comfortable living. It is then only that we shall experience the benefits of a just society.
Experts agree that, in order to live, a family must earn at least $3,000 a year. According to the 1961 census, 23 per cent of Canadian families did not earn that amount. On the other hand, the same experts say that, in Canada, more than 4,200,000 persons live in poverty. These figures are provided by the Economic Council of Canada.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, it is illogical and inconceivable to take off another $120 by way of a social development tax which is an added burden on individual budget and the people in the low income brackets. The modern poor is not only cast off by the present system, but he is made to pay the ransom of modern development of automation. To be poor today is not only to lack essential goods, but also to be unable to take part in social activities. Now, if we deprive the poor of his income, how can he take part in the life of our society?
Mr. Speaker, our government had a deficit of $422 million in 1966-67, and another of $792 million in 1967-68. The deficit will be approximately $675 million in 1968-69, but we were told it would be almost $700 million.
Mr. Speaker, government expenditures keep rising year after year. When calculating where each dollar collected by the federal government comes from, we find that the part which is the income tax collected from the little man, from the middle income people, from the one who can hardly make ends meet, also keeps rising.

To make sure, let us look at the following figures: in 1966-67, the federal government was collecting 28.5 cents as personal income tax. In 1967-68, for the same tax, the federal government asked for 31 cents, an increase of 3 cents. In 1968-69, the same tax continues to increase up to 32 cents.
We could make the same comparison with several other taxes: corporation income tax, sales tax, custom duties, taxes on alcohol, tobacco and so on. However, the more money the government takes out of the taxpayer's pocket, the more expenditures increase.
On one hand, Mr. Speaker, production is increasing, on the other hand, poverty and distress increase steadily, which proves that even the increase in productivity will not necessarily solve the problem of poverty and injustice in our society. In fact, that is where we find injustice: the figures quoted are rather eloquent.
Mr. Speaker, in the chapter on perspectives for the period from June 1968 to June 1969, it is said and I quote:
The economic growth of Canada, in the next twelve months will depend in part on the economic conditions in the United States and certain overseas countries.
Yet an official study was made on behalf of the federal government. It is known as the Watkins Report, tabled by Mr. Walter Gordon, former Liberal minister of finance, who was dismissed and boycotted as his views did not agree with those held by big finance.
Our Canadian governments are puppet governments. They do not hold the purse-strings.
They have but one power, that of getting more and more into debt, for the benefit of the financial sharks and to the prejudice of the individual. For instance, on page 132 of this same budget document, one can read the following as to the operations concerning the unmatured debt:
Unmatured debt transactions in 1967-68 reflected an increase of $788 million in unmatured debt outstanding in the hands of the public.
In 1966-67, the increase was of $711 million, which means, less the net book credit, an increase of $792 million of our net debt, for a bewildering total of $16,757 billion.
A deficit of $792 million is a record in rashness and improvidence. Canada is not its own master any more; we are accountants in the pay of a big finance that controls us, controls our life and our economy.
In such circumstances, in the face of the enormous and inexhaustible need for money, slavery can but increase at the service of the god of big finance.
November 8, 1968
